demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
She is 23, a young environmental scientist early in her career, and when she talks about her brother’s death she does so in a voice that is almost too steady, as if she is reading from a report she has memorized. Before he died, she says, she was the practical one in the family, the one who liked plans, field notes, and clean data. She had recently started a position that takes her to wetlands and industrial sites, collecting soil and water samples, logging contamination levels, and writing up findings for senior staff. She liked the order of it. Numbers made sense to her. The world, she believed, could be studied, tracked, and understood.

Her brother’s death breaks that assumption in an afternoon.

He is killed in a road traffic accident on his way home. She learns about it from a phone call that she at first mistakes for bad reception; she keeps asking the caller to repeat himself because the words do not fit together. At the hospital, she remembers fluorescent lights, the smell of disinfectant, a nurse touching her elbow, and the terrible unreality of seeing her mother fold in on herself. What she remembers most clearly is not his face but his shoes beside the bed. For weeks afterward, that detail returns to her without warning, vivid and intrusive, as if her mind has fastened onto the smallest part of the scene because the whole of it is unbearable.

In the first months after the funeral, she tells herself she must be strong. In her family, grief is shared but also disciplined; people gather, pray, bring food, speak about God’s will, and remind one another to endure. She goes back to work quickly because staying home is worse. At her desk she can stare at spreadsheets and maps, but concentration no longer comes easily. She reads the same paragraph of a site assessment three or four times. When her phone rings unexpectedly, her whole body jerks. If an unknown number appears on the screen, her heart starts pounding before she answers. Part of her is convinced that every call carries more disaster.

Fieldwork becomes especially difficult. On the road to sampling sites she watches every passing truck, every reckless overtake, every motorbike weaving through traffic. She sits rigid in the passenger seat, one hand braced against the door. If the driver brakes suddenly, a rush of heat shoots through her chest and she loses track of where she is for a second. She begins volunteering for more office-based tasks, telling colleagues she needs to focus on data analysis. It sounds reasonable, even ambitious, and no one questions it.

At night she sleeps lightly, if at all. Sometimes she dreams she is back in the hospital corridor, unable to reach her family. Sometimes in the dream her brother is alive but walking away from her, and she cannot make her legs move. She wakes drenched in sweat, listens for sounds in the house, and checks her phone to reassure herself that no one has called. Morning brings exhaustion rather than rest. She starts arriving late to work, then overcompensates by staying after hours, trying to recover the version of herself who was competent and calm.

She avoids more than she first admits. She takes a longer route to work to avoid the stretch of road where the accident happened. She stops looking at family photographs because if she sees his face, the rest of the day is gone. She rarely visits friends now; their laughter can feel almost insulting, and she dreads the moment someone asks, gently, how she is doing. When people say she is strong, she feels oddly irritated. Strength, to her, has come to mean going numb in public and unraveling in private.

What troubles her most is how changed she feels. She used to be curious and open, someone who enjoyed being outdoors for hours, attentive to birdsong, weather patterns, and the subtle changes in a landscape. Now she scans every environment for danger before she notices anything beautiful. Even at a marsh site, standing in hip boots with a sample bottle in hand, she finds herself listening not to wind or water but to distant engines, sirens, footsteps. Her body behaves as if catastrophe is always about to repeat itself.

She also carries a heavy sense of guilt that she recognizes as irrational but cannot shake. She thinks about the last conversation she had with her brother and replays it for hidden signs. She wonders whether she should have called him that day, whether some small act might have delayed him, rerouted him, saved him. She knows the logic does not hold, yet the thought loops endlessly.

Now, months later, her life appears intact from the outside. She is employed, productive enough, polite, composed. But she lives in a narrowed world organized around avoiding reminders, managing panic, and enduring unwanted memories that break through without permission. She says she misses her brother, but what emerges over several conversations is that she also misses herself—the young woman who once moved through the world assuming it was mostly safe.
